result.summary: Pausanias introduces the Altis and the great temple of Zeus at Olympia, giving its builder, sculptor, dimensions and dedications. He then describes the sculptures on its gables (the chariot race of Pelops and the battle of Lapiths and Centaurs) and the Labours of Hercules above the doors.

scenes.title: The Altis and the temple exterior
scenes.summary: Pausanias introduces Olympia, the Altis, the statue by Phidias, the temple's size, architect, marble tiles and the golden shields dedicated on it.

scenes.title: Gable sculptures
scenes.summary: The east gable shows the chariot race of Pelops and Oenomaus; the west shows the fight of Lapiths and Centaurs at Pirithous' wedding.

scenes.title: Labours of Hercules and interior
scenes.summary: Reliefs of Hercules' Labours above the doors, Iphitus crowned by Ecechiria, and the interior approach to the statue.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias names the Eleusinian mysteries and Olympic games as the clearest display of divine purpose.

analysis.text: Pausanias treats Olympia as a sacred centre where myth, art and civic memory meet, with sculpture recording legends such as Pelops and the Centaurs.
The dedications, from the spoils of Pisa to Mummius' shields, show how Greek sanctuaries recorded wars and political power.

legacy.text: The temple's gable sculptures, now in the Olympia museum, are central examples of Early Classical Greek sculpture.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias gives the temple as 230 feet long, and surviving foundations at Olympia confirm a very large building.

language_notes.text: Altis is a Doric form of the word for grove (alsos); Pausanias notes the wordplay. Pindar, the lyric poet, used the name in his victory odes.
Pisa was the district originally controlling Olympia. Elis crushed its revolt, and the spoils paid for the temple, a historical event the reader may not know.
Pentelican marble came from Mount Pentelicus near Athens and was prized for its fine white quality.
The Gorgon Medusa was a monster whose gaze turned people to stone; her head was a common protective emblem on shields.
Tanagra refers to a battle in Boeotia (457 BC) in which Sparta and allies defeated Athens; Lacedæmonians means Spartans.
Mummius sacked Corinth in 146 BC, ending the Achæan War; he dedicated spoils at Olympia.
Bas relief means sculpture carved to project only slightly from a flat background. Here the figures are actually free-standing; the translator's term is loose.
A charioteer drove the chariot; Myrtilus sits behind the four horses of the team.
"Tapers fine" means the narrowing corner of the triangular gable, where the reclining river figure fits.
Pausanias sets a local tradition against the Olympia guide's statement, showing he records conflicting accounts without deciding between them.
Homer calls Pirithous a son of Zeus in the Iliad; Pelops, who won Hippodamia in the race, links the myth to Olympia's own story.
Clearing the dung refers to the labour of cleaning the stables of Augeas, king of Elis, which is why it is placed at Olympia.
The Amazon's belt, the stag, Minotaur, Stymphalian birds, hydra and Nemean lion are further Labours; the Minotaur here means the Cretan bull.
Iphitus was the king credited with reviving the Olympic games; Ecechiria personifies the sacred truce kept during them.

context_notes.text: The Eleusinian mysteries were secret religious rites for Demeter and Persephone at Eleusis; the Olympian games honoured Zeus every four years.
Phidias was the celebrated Athenian sculptor whose enormous gold-and-ivory Zeus was counted among the Seven Wonders of the ancient world.
Doric was the plainest Greek architectural order, with sturdy fluted columns and undecorated capitals.
Alyattes ruled Lydia and Astyages ruled the Medes, both in the sixth century BC; the reference dates Byzes.
Oenomaus was king of Pisa who raced suitors for his daughter Hippodamia's hand and killed the losers; Pelops finally defeated him.
The Cladeus is a small river flowing past Olympia into the Alpheus, the region's greatest river.
Paeonius and Alcamenes were famous sculptors of the later fifth century BC; Phidias made the great statue of Zeus inside this temple.
The Centaurs, half-man half-horse, got drunk at the Lapith king Pirithous' wedding and tried to seize the women; the Lapiths defeated them.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias speaks as a travelling observer and pious Greek, framing Olympia as proof of divine purpose and setting a reverent tone.
The golden Victory crowning the gable symbolises triumph and the athletic and military glory the sanctuary celebrates.
The scene is balanced around Pirithous at the centre, with a rescuer on one side and Theseus on the other, mirroring the sculptural composition.
Pausanias offers his own conjecture with "I imagine", presenting himself as an interpreting traveller who reasons about the artist's intentions.
